name: Buttermilk Vanilla Waffles
headnote: Stella Parks makes the case for a deliberately lazy one-bowl waffle batter: no separating or whipping eggs, no separate wet and dry bowls, no sifting or folding. Her argument is that whipped whites exist to aerate batters that rise slowly in an oven, whereas a waffle is pressed between hot plates where steam does all the lifting, so hydration matters more than aeration. She builds the batter on buttermilk and egg whites only - moist and high in protein but lean, which gives structure and keeps the waffles crisp rather than cakey - uses powdered sugar because it dissolves smoothly, and adds only a pinch of baking soda, treating it as a seasoning that tempers the buttermilk's tang without cancelling it. Her main warning is not to overfill the iron, since batter that spreads outward cannot rise or vent its steam, and slightly ragged edges are a sign it had room to expand.
comment_digest: The single most useful correction addresses limp, flat waffles: one reviewer traced the problem to thin store-bought buttermilk, noting Stella's is thick and creamy and that homemade milk-plus-vinegar substitutes make the batter too loose, and reports that switching to kefir produced crisp, airy results. Flavored kefir also works and doubles as a flavoring - blueberry kefir plus frozen berries adds flavor and, because the batter goes in very cold, slows cooking and browns the waffles better. Granulated sugar can stand in for powdered if it is whisked into the liquid first so it dissolves, and vanilla extract substitutes acceptably for the bean, though several say the bean is noticeably better. The recipe halves cleanly. Some cut the sugar by half. The waffles are reported to freeze and reheat well. One open question, unanswered, is whether any egg substitute works for the whites.
